chapter: Opening and life on the road
title: Utica quartet gig: bringing arrangements, missing the bass
summary: He explains why he brought music stands and arrangements to the pickup quartet, and how the absence of a bassist left the band without bottom.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Well I noticed something today that I liked and I thought was interesting, and that I should tell our readers and viewers that I just saw you perform in Utica, with a typical sort of assembled group, you know, a quartet that had never performed together before. But you guys had a couple of music stands, which doesn’t always happen. Was that your doing?

Uh, well I think for me I like to get into a situation and not necessarily just winging it and calling tunes, I like to bring some arrangements and try and do something, you know, present something with a little more formality and something that’s less just thrown together haphazardly, even though I do enjoy that situation as well, um just winging it and getting on the stage and figuring out what you’re going to play. We did have the luxury of a short rehearsal and, like I was telling the folks who came out to The Other Side, at the gig this afternoon, is that, you know, jazz is a language and it’s like any other language. And if you learn to speak the language you can play with almost anybody. So you know the level of musicianship is high in this area. I mean there’s people that can really play. The only thing I was missing, unfortunately, was a bass, because either through budgetary constraints or, I don’t know what the reason was, you know the pianist was —

Was playing bass as well as piano. Just in terms from a sound point of view, you don’t really get the bottom in the band that you would if you had a bass player playing. That’s, for me, something’s really missing without the bass. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-
